articles.title_orig: Utah files criminal charges against prediction market Kalshi and company co-founders
articles.title_zh: Utah files criminal charges against prediction market Kalshi and company co-founders
articles.content_orig:
Firm calls charges, which include violating state gambling ban and profiting from illegal activity, ‘crazy overreach’
Utah on Wednesday filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity.
The felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the US supreme court.
The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.
The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara.
In a statement, Utah attorney general Derek Brown said Kalshi has continued to operate in Utah, despite a federal court ruling that Utah’s gambling laws apply to the company.
“Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a ‘prediction market’ doesn’t change what it is, and being federally registered doesn’t put a company above the law,” Brown said in a statement.
The attorney general’s office did not immediately say what sort of criminal penalties it would seek in the case, although the felony charges carry the possibility of jail time.
In a statement, Kalshi called the charges a “crazy overreach” and said that “Utah is clearly playing politics”.
“We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” it said.
Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across roughly 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the supreme court.
Kalshi has maintained that prediction markets fall exclusively under federal jurisdiction and are not governed by state gambling laws.

articles.title_orig: Chinese boy who donated US$1.5 to end power cuts now works for energy company
articles.title_zh: Chinese boy who donated US$1.5 to end power cuts now works for energy company
articles.content_orig:
Feeling that his first contribution was far too small for such a massive undertaking, Wang quietly made a second US$1.5 donation shortly after
A boy in central China who donated 10 yuan (US$1.5) to the Three Gorges Dam project in the 1990s now works for the power grid, helping transmit the electricity it generates across the country.
Wang Yu, 47, works for the State Grid Corporation of China in his hometown of Zigui county, Hubei province, according to Hubei Daily.
In 1991, 12-year-old Wang received a daily allowance of just one yuan – barely enough to buy breakfast – at a time when his parents earned a combined monthly salary of less than 100 yuan (US$15).

articles.title_orig: US should spy on Chinese firms to maintain edge in tech race: ex-CIA official
articles.title_zh: US should spy on Chinese firms to maintain edge in tech race: ex-CIA official
articles.content_orig:
Former CIA deputy director’s call to repeal Obama-era ban on economic espionage comes as Beijing rushes to protect trade secrets
A former CIA official has called for Washington to spy on foreign companies to help US firms stay ahead in the technology race, in what would represent a break from long-standing US policy amid intensifying competition with China.
“The US lead in many crucial advanced technologies is being contested or even erased by China,” wrote David Cohen, who served as deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, in an article published by Foreign Affairs earlier this month.
“By abstaining from economic espionage, the United States has tilted the playing field against itself and magnified the Chinese threat.”

articles.title_orig: Breaking News: Google eyeing data center campus in Goochland’s West Creek
articles.title_zh: Breaking News: Google eyeing data center campus in Goochland’s West Creek
articles.content_orig:
Left: a map of three of four potential data center developments in Goochland County. Right: a map of the subject property for a potential 1,200-megawatt development within the TOD that Google is seemingly interested in. (Courtesy State Corporation Commission filings)
Note: This is an update to a breaking news alert first published Wednesday afternoon.
Google has its sights set on Goochland for yet another potential data center project in the Richmond region.
The tech giant is considering the purchase of a roughly 1,000-acre site in West Creek Business Park, where it would build a 1,200-megawatt data center campus, the company confirmed Wednesday after a news release from the county.
Because the property sits within the county’s recently approved technology overlay district, or TOD, any data center project on the site would be a by-right use and would not need to go through the public hearing process.
Google is in the process of performing due diligence on the property. If it decides to move forward with the project and purchase the land, the next step would be to begin site engineering to develop a site plan to submit to the county.
As of now, Google has submitted no plans, Goochland County Administrator Jeremy Raley said in an email Wednesday.
The project site would bisect Route 288 north of Patterson Avenue and is owned by an entity tied to Pruitt Associates and Riverstone Group, which control the bulk of the land in West Creek.
A map of Goochland’s TOD district. (Courtesy Goochland County)
Wednesday’s release from the county was the first time Google has been associated with the proposed project.
It was first mentioned, without identifying Google, in a State Corporation Commission regulatory filing from July 14, which listed several potential data center campuses proposed by mystery applicants for the eastern portion of Goochland.
Those include Google’s potential 1,200-megawatt project, a 600-megawatt project that would rise on roughly 150 acres off Ashland Road, and a 200-megawatt project east of Route 288 and north of Patterson Avenue.
All three data center developments mentioned in the July filing are located in the TOD and an accompanying technology zone, which together span about 5 miles along Route 288, from Interstate 64 south to Patterson Avenue. The TOD area is bordered to the west by Hockett Road and spans roughly 4,400 acres, with about 3,500 of those acres within West Creek, controlled by Pruitt Associates.
According to the July filing, the “customer” for the 1,200-megawatt data center campus had “executed four ELOAs,” or engineering letters of authorization, for the project. After an ELOA is issued, projects are placed in a project queue for Dominion Energy, where it can sit for years before a feasibility study is done on a site and a construction letter of authorization, or CLOA, is executed.
It was not specified in the SCC filing who the 1,200-megawatt campus customer was, but Google officials confirmed to BizSense Wednesday that it was interested in that site specifically.
The county in its release said conversations with Google aren’t new. The release details a timeline of events, starting with the Virginia Economic Development Partnership reaching out to the county in early 2024 to “meet with a data center user and show them potential sites in Goochland County.”
Google data center in Oregon. (Courtesy Google)
The release states that the county entered into a nondisclosure agreement with Google on Jan. 10, 2024, and that county staff had one meeting with Google officials to discuss potential locations for a data center development on Jan. 30 of that year.
“After the meeting, VEDP told the County that Google was not interested and was not moving forward. There was no further communication with Google at that time,” the release reads.
However, after last November’s adoption of the TOD, Google reengaged with the county and began due diligence on the West Creek site.
“Since the County was already under NDA from previous discussions, the County did not enter into a new NDA,” the release says.
In what the county said was an effort to provide transparency, it requested to be released from the NDA, and yesterday, both the county and Google agreed to the release, prompting Wednesday’s announcement of Google’s involvement.
The potential Google site is east of the proposed Tuckahoe Tech Park, which would rise within the county’s TOD West area, a 900-acre tract where data centers require a conditional-use permit.
Denver, Colorado-based data center developer Tract is behind that project. The project would need approvals through the public hearing process before being able to move forward.
The announcement of Google’s interest in West Creek comes shortly after a recent hearing in a lawsuit four Goochland residents have brought against the county, claiming supervisors and planning commissioners failed to clearly and lawfully explain their adoption of the TOD.
A hearing last Tuesday addressed the county’s motion to dismiss the residents’ lawsuit. That motion is under advisement by the judge in the case.
Google’s efforts in Goochland would add to its already sizable data center aspirations in the Richmond region.
The company has begun construction on a data center campus on a 300-plus-acre site at 2700 Bermuda Hundred Road in eastern Chesterfield next to Meadowville Technology Park, and has several other data center facilities planned for the western end of Chesterfield County.

articles.title_orig: Weil Gotshal, Once a Legal Powerhouse, Plans to Dissolve
articles.title_zh: Weil Gotshal, Once a Legal Powerhouse, Plans to Dissolve
articles.content_orig:
Leaders at Weil, Gotshal & Manges, the nearly century-old law firm that worked for companies from the Lehman Brothers to General Motors, recommended on Wednesday that the firm shut down.
“Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm’s Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down,” a Weil spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.
The firm’s partners are expected to vote on the recommendation “in the coming days,” according to the statement. Equity partners hold stakes in law firms and can vote on company matters.
For over 90 years, the law firm was well-known through Wall Street for steering high-profile corporate litigation such as bankruptcies and mergers. Weil advised the Lehman Brothers during the 2008 financial crisis, and the firm claims it brought General Motors out of bankruptcy in “just 40 days.”
The firm said it guided debtors such as Enron, whose 2001 bankruptcy filing was the largest in American history at the time. It also advised Microsoft’s $68.7 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard as well as AT&T’s acquisition of DirecTV .
The firm had been mired by an exodus of prominent partners, largely driven by competition from rivals, legal news outlet Law.com earlier reported . And a potential merger with another law firm, Willkie Farr, fell through this year.
Weil is announcing its closure without filing for bankruptcy.
The news sent shockwaves through the Big Law industry, which has been going through its own changes. Big mergers and acquisitions have led to more competition for top talent – and then there’s the looming dread of artificial intelligence.
Weil was founded in 1931 and employs approximately 1,200 lawyers in offices from New York to Munich to Hong Kong, according to its website. The firm did not announce plans for its employees or office spaces on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices fall as peace hopes offset fears of growing Middle East conflict
articles.title_zh: Oil prices fall as peace hopes offset fears of growing Middle East conflict
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Oil prices edged up about 1% on Wednesday on renewed concerns about additional energy supply disruptions in the Middle East due to continued fighting in Yemen, an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia and worries ‌the US could strike Iran after next week's US midterm elections.
Brent futures rose $1.44, or 1%, to settle at $115.32 per barrel, while US West Texas ‌Intermediate crude rose $2.88, or 3%, to settle at $102.78.
That price gain pushed Brent back into overbought territory for the fourth time in five days.
Yemen's Houthis attacked Aden airport on Wednesday, Yemeni government forces ​said, after the Iran-aligned group warned people to evacuate the facility as fighting escalated in the impoverished country caught in the wider Middle East conflict.
On Tuesday, the Houthis said they had hit Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery with a missile, intensifying their strikes against the world's second-largest crude producer behind the US. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike on the 550,000-barrel-per-day facility.
"Crude futures once again pricing in nearer term tighter supplies on news the US is likely to re-start military ‌operations soon, which could be more intense than in ⁠the past given the latest attacks on Saudi Arabia and other Middle East allies," Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at US financial services firm BOK Financial, said in a note.
In recent weeks, several analysts have said renewed US ⁠strikes on Iran could happen sometime after the US midterm elections on November 3.
In hopes of ending the now eight-month-long conflict, Qatari mediators have presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations said. A senior Iranian official, however, said Doha had only ​put ​forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
Iran's foreign minister said on ​Wednesday that Tehran continued to give diplomacy a chance to succeed ‌and raised the possibility of the seven-day plan proposed by Tehran being completed in less than a week if implemented.
Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war, which has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and has spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
Another factor supporting crude prices was a US federal report showing a surprise decline in stockpiles.
The US Energy Information Administration said on Wednesday that energy firms pulled 1.9 million barrels of crude from storage during the week ended October 23.
That was a surprise draw compared with the 15,000-barrel build analysts forecast in a Reuters poll, and was ‌in line with the 2-million-barrel decline seen in data from the American Petroleum Institute on ​Tuesday, according to sources. [EIA/S] [API/S]
China, meanwhile, issued a fourth batch of fuel export quotas for gasoline, ​diesel and jet fuel, a rare additional issue that brings the ​2026 total in line with 2025 despite curbs earlier in the year, three people familiar with the matter said ‌on Wednesday.
Looking ahead, the market is waiting for an industry meeting ​on Sunday, where OPEC+ oil producers are ​expected to keep their December oil output targets steady, people familiar with the matter said.
Production in most of the seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — is below their output targets. OPEC+ includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries ​and allies like Russia.
Crude oil exports from Russia's Baltic ‌and Black Sea ports could fall next month as domestic refiners increase diesel output following a deal with Washington this month, traders ​said.
(Reporting by Scott DiSavino in New York, Stephanie Kelly in London and Jeslyn Lerh in Singapore; Additional reporting by Colleen Howe ​in Beijing; Editing by Christian Schmollinger, Joe Bavier, Mark Potter and Bill Berkrot)

articles.title_orig: High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say
articles.title_zh: High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say
articles.content_orig:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain , derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Padilla told state broadcaster TVE the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January. Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focused on rescuing survivors and bodies from the most damaged train cars.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
One passenger said, "We were all thrown into the air." He said he was "reasonably OK" but that his friend was in much worse condition.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.
In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

articles.title_orig: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady
articles.title_zh: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady
articles.content_orig:
The cost of living is Issue No. 1 for voters heading to the polls, but the Federal Reserve saw America’s persistent inflation problem Wednesday and opted not to do anything about it.
At least for the next six weeks, anyway.
Despite consumer prices gaining 3.7% over the past year and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge stubbornly remaining 50% above the central bank’s target, the decision to hold interest rates steady was widely expected.
That’s because changing rates is a blunt instrument that can inflict serious damage on the economy when ill-timed or used improperly.
“Interest rates get in the cracks,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a press briefing Wednesday. “They affect everything.”
Central bankers just last month hiked rates for the first time in more than three years, and they want to wait a bit to see how the economy responds before bashing it over the head again with another rate hike.
“Ensuring price stability and watching inflation is not about some fixed date on a calendar or some isolated data point,” Warsh said. “It’s about ensuring we have clear objectives and the right monetary policy.”
Warsh said he was encouraged by the reduction in inflation expectations since the Fed raised rates in September.
By waiting, however, the Fed is also taking a significant gamble. The Fed risks another 2021-like mistake, when it assumed the inflation monster staring the economy directly in the face could be defeated by just ignoring it. (The Fed was disastrously wrong).
This time may truly be different, and not acting with haste could prove prescient.
Or it could force the central bank to give the economy some December shock therapy that it may have been able to avoid with an October rate hike.
Jobs. Hiking rates increases businesses’ borrowing costs, which leaves them with less money to hire.
Now may be a perilous time to mess with the job market: The US economy added only 29,000 jobs in September, well below expectations. And the September report showed that the economy added 60,000 fewer jobs over the previous two months than previously believed.
The labor market is by no means in bad shape, but it has been on shaky ground. The US economy lost 10,000 jobs in July and in seven of the past 16 months. Although unemployment remains at a healthy 4.2%, economists describe the economy as “low hire, low fire.”
In other words, your position may not be at risk, but if you leave your job, you may have trouble finding a new one.
Markets. Treasury yields moved higher since the last Fed rate hike, with bond yields at one point hitting multi-decade highs. Yields have slipped a bit since, returning to where they were in mid-September, but the still relatively high bond yields can help give the Fed cover, because they have an effect similar to the Fed funds rate, slowing the economy and inflation.
The Fed also doesn’t like to surprise investors – even in Warsh’s new keep-‘em-guessing era. The market had priced in a 91% chance that the Fed would hold rates, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, and a hike could have sent the markets into a painful rebalancing.
Timing. The Fed’s decision may also have been influenced, at least somewhat, by the upcoming election. Narayana Kocherlakota, the former Minneapolis Fed president, told my colleague Matt Egan that the Fed hesitated to raise rates Wednesday because it wanted insulation from President Donald Trump’s criticism. But the Fed throughout its history has changed rates many times just as voters were heading to the polls, my colleague Elisabeth Buchwald also noted .
The “transitory” error: The Fed typically doesn’t get involved when supply shocks like the Iran-war-induced energy crisis cause inflation. They’re notoriously temporary, hard to predict and insensitive to rate changes.
But supply shocks sometimes lead to bigger problems that the Fed can help fix. The Fed should know: It just went through this.
As the economy emerged from the pandemic, the Fed made a mistake with inflation, declaring it a result of a “transitory” supply shock related to the Russia-Ukraine war and massive supply chain snarls. It ended up becoming the most significant inflation problem in a generation. The Fed, caught off guard, was forced to raise rates at a historic pace – three consecutive hikes of three-quarters of a percentage point.
Ultimately, the Fed succeeded at lowering out-of-control inflation to more manageable levels, but not before consumer prices peaked at an annual rate of 9.1%, the highest in four decades.
This time may be no different: Inflation is already spilling over into other parts of the economy.
Particularly concerning in the September consumer inflation report was the surprising rebound in housing and rent costs, a significant contributor to inflation that had cooled off in the spring and summer. And the cost of other services rose higher than expected, too – prices that tend to rise (and stay high) as yoga studios, lawn services and the like charge their customers more to make up for their rising costs.
Also driving inflation: Investment in data centers and technology powering AI has propelled the economy into overdrive – and maybe helped overheat it. Prices for electricity, building materials, labor, and personal tech like smartphones and laptops have all risen as a result.
More war? This energy price spike could get worse before it gets better. Trump has strongly hinted (and CNN has reported ) that the United States and Israel could escalate the war with Iran after the midterm elections, potentially sending oil prices higher.
It would be foolhardy for the Fed to make a decision based on a rumor. And energy prices can quickly swing lower. For example, the Trump administration’s announcement of an energy ceasefire in Russia has held surprisingly well, dramatically increasing the amount of diesel Russia produced in the past couple weeks, which could significantly lower global diesel prices – if Ukraine continues to hold off on its drone strikes on Russian refineries.
But the prolonged energy price spike is already raising prices across the economy, and waiting to hike again could place the Fed behind the curve.
Boiling frogs. Rate hikes work with a delayed effect, and sharper rate changes can have deleterious effects on the financial system, markets and the economy. This economic frog tends to stay in the pot when the heat is turned up gradually.
If escalations in the Iran war and Russia-Ukraine war resume, that could force the Fed into a difficult position of hiking rates by even more than expected in its next meeting in December – potentially by a half point, in a kind of make-up call.
The massive, successive rate hikes throughout 2022 sent the stock market into its biggest annual decline since the financial crisis and put the housing market on ice. But the economy didn’t go into a recession – a trick the Fed has rarely pulled off when it hikes rates.
It’s not a wager a lot of economists are eager to place again.

articles.title_orig: US and Japan, long alarmed by China’s aggression, agree to establish missile-production facility
articles.title_zh: US and Japan, long alarmed by China’s aggression, agree to establish missile-production facility
articles.content_orig:
US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title_orig: Inside India newsletter: New Delhi approves $22 billion in military spending amid China border tensions
articles.title_zh: Inside India newsletter: New Delhi approves $22 billion in military spending amid China border tensions
articles.content_orig:
Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.
Welcome to the latest edition of " Inside India " — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.
India, the world's fifth-largest military spender, shares a contentious relationship with two of its nuclear-armed neighbors — China and Pakistan. Last year, New Delhi carried out military strikes against alleged terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan, and last week an Indian official confirmed some border clashes with China.
As tensions at its borders simmer, India this week announced plans to spend billions of dollars on procuring modern warfare equipment. From whom will it get the goods?
Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.
The world's second-largest arms importer, India, is pouring billions of dollars into modernizing its military as it seeks to counter the technological advancements of neighboring China, with whom it shares an uneasy peace.
Last week, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's north-eastern border.
Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor, the director general of a division of India's central armed forces, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, also called China the "biggest adversary" and urged for modernization of defense equipment. "It will be difficult to compete with China using traditional methods," Kapoor said.
Following Kapoor's comments, India approved spending 2.12 trillion rupees ($22 billion) to modernize its defense equipment on Monday. The country plans to spend on long-range kamikaze drones, surveillance and strike systems, counter-drone technologies, short-range air defense, artillery, helicopters and naval platforms.
Experts told CNBC that New Delhi increasingly views Beijing as a threat, especially given the Sino-Pakistan military ties, and the latest purchases were aimed at bridging the technological gap with China.
A spokesperson for India's foreign ministry said on Friday that "the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns." Beijing responded, saying it "strictly abides by the relevant agreements and common understandings reached between the two countries."
India's military policies are largely driven by its long-standing conflict with Pakistan, and an "increasing perception of China as a threat," Pieter Wezeman, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told CNBC.
According to a SIPRI report earlier this year, 61% of Chinese arms exports were supplied to Pakistan between 2021 and 2025.
India's latest weapons purchases will involve importing components and technology from South Korea for the artillery, engines and avionics from France for the helicopters, and drones from the U.S. and Israel, Wezeman said.
Collaboration with Russia and Japan could also be on the cards, given India's need for a technological upgrade.
Since April, India has greenlighted military spending totaling 3.7 trillion rupees, which is more than 50% of the 6.73 trillion rupee worth of approvals — a 10-year high — in the financial year ended March 2026, Citi said in a report on Tuesday.
While New Delhi has said it plans to procure 82% of the defense equipment from local industries, foreign companies are likely to play a key role in providing technology crucial for military modernization.
Foreign partnerships remain important for technologies that India does not yet produce independently, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo, told CNBC. India relies on imported technologies for specialized components such as aircraft engines, propulsion systems, sensors and electronic subsystems, he explained.
"American, Israeli, and Russian defense manufacturers are likely to find substantial opportunities in India's expanding defense market," through joint ventures, co-production and technology partnerships with Indian companies, Chaturvedi said.
India was the world's second-largest importer of major arms in 2021–25 with an 8.2% share of total global imports, even as its reliance on overseas suppliers dropped by 4% during the same time due to growing local design and production abilities, according to SIPRI.
New Delhi is also the world's fifth-largest military spender, with $92 billion, but this is less than 30% of Chinese military expenditure and around a 10th of America's, Wezeman of SIPRI pointed out.
India faces some practical challenges in matching China's scale of military modernization, but the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have shown that mass-produced systems like drones can address asymmetry, Collin Koh Swee Lean, a senior fellow at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, said.

articles.title_orig: They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
articles.title_zh: They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
articles.content_orig:
A residential cruise ship halted operations in Cambodia on Tuesday amid soaring fuel costs , leaving passengers in limbo after the U.S. company that operates it ordered them to disembark.
Florida-based Villa Vie Residences said in a news release that it was working to identify “temporary living arrangements” for people aboard The Odyssey, a 642-foot cruise ship that launched from Belfast, Northern Ireland, three years ago and promised passengers “an unparalleled lifestyle of luxury and exploration” as it toured the planet.
Cabins on The Odyssey were for sale or rent.
According to the company , the ship can accommodate 650 residents. A Cambodian official said Wednesday there were 203 passengers and 156 ​crew members on the ship. Some passengers had already departed on ​flights, while others were waiting in the port city of Sihanoukville, Long Dimanche, deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk Province, told media.
The ship is scheduled to refuel before leaving ‌Cambodia on ⁠Saturday, he added.
An executive with the company, Mikael Petterson, declined to provide additional details in an email to NBC News. In a release this year announcing the company’s second residential cruise ship, Petterson said The Odyssey was 85% sold.
The company said in Tuesday’s release that it had taken significant measures to reduce fuel consumption but that those steps had failed to offset the spike in costs.
Global oil prices have surged since the war with Iran began this year, disrupting the world’s flow of fuel. In recent days, oil prices have climbed to their highest levels in months.
“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said. “Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured.”
Randy Cassingham, a resident on the vessel, wrote in a blog post that he learned his journey was over after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship shortly after 7 a.m. Monday.
The Odyssey was entering a “temporary lay up” period — indicating it would no longer be used — and everyone had to disembark by 2 p.m., the message said, according to Cassingham, who runs ResidentialCruising.com and didn’t immediately reply to an interview request.
Cassingham attributed the development to a “cascade of problems” that he would detail later.
Pamela Reckamp, who rented a cabin with her husband and disembarked this month, said in an interview that she wasn’t surprised that the ship’s journey was over.
Reckamp, 59, recalled having attended a meeting in early September at which a company official asked cabin owners to help them raise $1 million so they could leave Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.
“She said, ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp recalled. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”
When the ship’s financial issues were raised during another meeting a few weeks later, Reckamp recalled, a woman stood up and said she’d bought a cabin in August and hadn’t been made aware of the issues.
“I sold my house,” Reckamp recalled the woman saying. “I sold my car. I bought my home on this ship.”
Residential cruise ship halts operations over fuel costs
Reckamp said she felt terrible for the residents and the staff, who she said were lovely.
“We dodged a bullet,” she added.
Villa Vie Residences didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday night.
In a lawsuit filed last year, a company that bought a cabin on The Odyssey for $469,000 accused Villa Vie Residences of fraud, alleging it misrepresented its financial stability.
The company’s business model was not financially sound, the suit alleges, “but rather precarious.”
The plaintiffs are asking for a jury trial and unspecified damages of more than $100,000. Villa Vie Residences denied the allegations in the suit, which is ongoing.
Other cabins on the ship were available for significantly less money. Even though 85% of the ship was sold, the company said in 2024, prospective residents could still “secure their dream home starting at just $119,000.”
“When we launched Odyssey, we set out to prove that residential cruising wasn’t just possible — it was sustainable,” Petterson said in July.
Tim Stelloh is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Couple who lived on cruise ship for 2 years forced off in Cambodia after company halts operations
articles.title_zh: Couple who lived on cruise ship for 2 years forced off in Cambodia after company halts operations
articles.content_orig:
Passengers on a live-aboard round-the-world cruise say they were abruptly asked to leave the ship and given only hours to disembark.
Villa Vie Residences, which operates the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey , said on Tuesday it had halted operations due to surging fuel costs.
The ship was docked at the port of Sihanoukville in Cambodia when the announcement was made, with passengers saying they were given only eight hours to disembark.
"On October 27, 2026, we received notice from the CEO at around 6 a.m. that all residents had to disembark by 2 p.m. that day," passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told Business Insider by email.
Canen and Bodin have been on the Odyssey since it first set sail in September 2024 and run a YouTube channel called Living Life on a Cruise about their experiences on board.
"We knew leaving was a possibility, but the eight-hour notice still surprised us," they said.
The couple shared a video on their YouTube channel that appears to show the moment a staff member announced that passengers must leave the ship.
"Unfortunately, they were unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations," a male voice says in the video.
A notice on the Villa Vie Residences website says the company is working with residents to arrange temporary living arrangements and that it is evaluating restructuring options over the next 60 days.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Mikael Petterson, executive chairman of Villa Vie Residences, told Business Insider he understood residents' feelings of shock and sadness.
"I get it. I get it. I feel awful," he said in a phone interview. "They're counting on me to make the decisions here and there's nothing else I'm focused on. I'm the villain in the story, but I'm doing everything I can to support the residents on a solution forward."
Petterson said that until last week, he was in talks with a potential investor and was expecting a new infusion of cash. When the deal fell apart, he said, the company was out of options.
Villa Vie Residences Chief Executive Kathy Villalba didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
Villa Vie Residences said in a statement Tuesday that the surging cost of fuel since the beginning of the Iran war had made operating the cruise liner increasingly difficult.
The company said its monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which had previously averaged about $1,800, had risen as much as 344% in parts of Asia, to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000.
"Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port," Villa Vie Residences said.
"Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
On August 1, Villalba, the CEO, sent residents a message titled "Urgent operational update" on an internal messaging platform. In the message, she referenced a "fuel contribution" that had been previously requested of residents. Business Insider has viewed a screenshot of the message.
"When the fuel contribution was requested several months ago, participation was not universal," she wrote in the message. "The contributions received helped some, but they covered only part of the extraordinary increase in fuel costs."
Villalba wrote that the "cash-flow" challenge had continued, and the Odyssey needed 650 metric tons of fuel, adding that fuel prices had almost doubled.
"We have now reached a critical point. The lack of full participation, combined with the unprecedented increase in fuel costs, means we must make immediate and creative operational decisions to preserve the voyage," her message said.
It continued, "We are asking every Resident who did not previously contribute to please do so now. We are also asking those who are able to provide additional support to consider helping with this immediate fuel requirement."
Villalba described the financial need as "real, immediate, and necessary to keep Odyssey moving." It went on, "This is a moment when preserving our home and continuing the voyage requires support beyond contractual minimums from those who are able to provide it."
Among the passengers asked to disembark on Tuesday with only a few hours' notice was Barbara Fiegel, 62, who has lived with her partner aboard the ship since December 2024.
"Everybody's just shocked, everybody's just saddened by this whole issue," she said. "We're still processing, trying to debate what we're going to do."
Fiegel said she and her partner booked a hotel room in Cambodia, then returned to the ship Tuesday evening and Wednesday afternoon to empty their safe and pack their belongings. "Today, as we approached, as we went back on the shuttle back to the ship, I couldn't stop crying," she said.
They plan to return on Thursday to collect their remaining items. Fiegel described the atmosphere on the Odyssey as a “ghost town.”
Joel Greiff, 57, moved aboard the ship at the start of the month and planned to live on the ship for 10 or 20 years or more. “I don’t think that will be happening,” he said.
When residents were told to disembark, Greiff emptied his cabin. “I personally grabbed everything,” he said.
He said he would like to return if Villa Vie Residences resumes operations. If not, he is planning to move to Thailand. In the meantime, he has rented an apartment in Cambodia for a month.
Greiff said he plans to return to the Odyssey on Thursday to assist other residents and “help with their luggage, help them find a place, and just start getting them and all their stuff off the ship.”
Jacob Shamsian contributed to this story.
Have you spent any time on the Villa Vie Odyssey as a cabin owner, renter, or staff member? If you have a story to share, get in touch with this reporter: jzitser@businessinsider.com .
Correction: October 28, 2026 — An earlier version of this story misspelled Johan Bodin's name.

articles.title_orig: One passport isn’t enough for some wealthy Chinese. Here’s where they’re looking next
articles.title_zh: One passport isn’t enough for some wealthy Chinese. Here’s where they’re looking next
articles.content_orig:
For some wealthy Chinese, securing a foreign passport is becoming the ultimate trade-off: giving up their Chinese citizenship.
Wealth advisors say a growing number of affluent Chinese are considering renouncing their nationality as Beijing intensifies scrutiny of offshore wealth, with concerns over taxes, geopolitical uncertainty and greater international mobility driving their interest in alternative passports.
China does not recognize dual nationality, meaning Chinese nationals seeking to acquire foreign citizenship must renounce their passports.
"We have had some clients who are willing to give up their Chinese citizenship to hold multiple passports," said Armand Arton, CEO of immigration migration consultancy Arton Capital, who added that the choice of passports depends on their lifestyle and business needs.
Meanwhile, Ryan Lin, director at Singapore-based legal firm Bayfront Law, said he has seen an increase in wealthy Chinese considering renouncing their nationality since July.
That month, Beijing introduced new measures targeting offshore trusts, with certain incomes and transactions potentially subject to a 20% tax. The changes have prompted some families to reassess how they hold and transfer assets overseas.
Previously, clients would discuss the possibility of giving up their citizenship. Now, more are expressing concrete intentions to do so, Lin told CNBC.
Manish Tibrewal, co-founder of multi-family office Farro Capital, also reported growing interest in foreign passports.
The wealth advisory firm is helping some Chinese families pursue Caribbean citizenship alongside Singapore permanent residency, with the longer-term possibility of obtaining Singapore citizenship, subject to government approval.
Tibrewal said the number of Chinese families actively exploring alternative citizenship options since July far exceeds those who have completed the process last year.
Inquiries from Chinese clients have risen 33% since July, investment migration firm Savory & Partners said, while Global Citizen Solutions reported an increase of nearly 40% compared with the same period last year.
Both firms specialize in investment migration, which helps wealthy individuals obtain foreign residency or citizenship, often through qualifying investments in their destination countries.
Renouncing Chinese citizenship does not automatically erase existing tax liabilities though.
Individuals could remain liable for taxes on historical gains, depending on how their wealth was structured, even after giving up their nationality, but a genuine change in citizenship and residency could affect future obligations, experts said.
For many wealthy Chinese, relinquishing their nationality remains a significant sacrifice, particularly for those whose businesses and fortunes are tied to the mainland.
Lin said those most willing to take that step generally have few remaining business links to China, with much of their wealth and operations already based offshore.
So where are they looking to move?
For wealthy Chinese seeking an alternative passport rather than merely overseas residency, the Caribbean has emerged as a popular choice.
Countries such as Antigua and Barbuda offer citizenship-by-investment programs that allow eligible applicants to obtain nationality through qualifying investments or contributions.
Tibrewal said Caribbean citizenship can potentially be secured within six months, making it considerably faster than pathways in Europe or the United States, where residency requirements often precede naturalization.
Arton said the appeal is less about permanently relocating and more about greater flexibility to travel and establish an international base.
Global Citizen Solutions said the Caribbean recorded the strongest growth in Chinese inquiries among the destinations it tracked this year.
European countries are also attracting interest, although many offer residency pathways rather than immediate citizenship.
"For Chinese HNWIs who are not willing to give up their citizenship, a portfolio of residencies or long-term visas is a more appealing option," Arton said.
Portugal remains popular through its golden visa program, which offers residency through qualifying investments and a potential longer-term route to citizenship.
Arton also added that Italy is attracting wealthy families through its favorable tax arrangements for qualifying new residents, international schools and financial services infrastructure.
Hungary is another emerging destination, offering long-term residency through qualifying investments starting at 250,000 euros ($290,000).
“Hungary is the one that surprises people,” according to Global Citizen Solutions. “As the larger European golden visa routes have closed or become more expensive, Hungary offers residency in the Schengen area through a regulated fund investment.”
Singapore remains attractive to wealthy Chinese because of its political stability, established wealth management industry, international schools and proximity to mainland China.
Some families are pursuing Singapore permanent residency as part of longer-term citizenship plans, although naturalization is neither automatic nor guaranteed.
Tibrewal said his firm was assisting some clients with plans involving Caribbean citizenship and Singapore residency, with Singapore citizenship a possible longer-term objective.
Australia is another popular option, particularly for families prioritizing education and quality of life.
Malaysia is also gaining attention, especially Kuala Lumpur and Penang, where lower living costs, Chinese-speaking communities and international schools appeal to families, said the migration consultancies.
"We also see interest beyond the obvious hubs in Asia, including Penang and Thailand's long-term resident visa, from families who value lifestyle and lower costs," said Global Citizen Solutions.
Meanwhile, Argentina and parts of Eastern Europe are emerging as alternative destinations for those seeking to diversify their international residency options.
Arton Capital identified Argentina as a market worth watching, while Savory & Partners highlighted growing interest in Serbia, North Macedonia and Bulgaria.
Advisors caution that interest in overseas citizenship does not necessarily translate into completed renunciations or physical relocations.
"It's important to recognize that exploring overseas residency, building a passport portfolio, and relocating an entire family are very different decisions," Arton said.

Supporters of Israel's Arab-led Joint List political alliance cheer at the alliance's campaign headquarters in the northern Israeli city of Nazareth  on October 27, 2026, as the first exit polls are announced.
                                          | Photo Credit: AFP
Israel’s October 27 legislative elections recorded a massive voter turnout of 77.7%, the highest since 1999. The country’s Arab citizens, who turned up in massive numbers to vote, remained one of the main factors, contributing to the surge.
While the official figures for voter turnout among Israeli Arabs are yet to be released by the Central Elections Committee, exit polls recorded by Channel 12 estimate Arab voter turnout to be nearly 80%. This implies that the voter turnout among Arab citizens in Israel would be the highest in at least a decade.
Also Read | Israel elections: Understanding how Knesset polls work vs India’s system
While Arabs account for about 21% of Israel’s population, the parties representing them have never held more than 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset. Their turnout in the elections has also been relatively low, with about 40% of eligible Arab adults abstaining from voting in most Knesset elections over the past two decades.
“In the previous elections, I think the low voter turnout was a result of disappointment mainly from Arab parties themselves. We know that approximately 10% of Arab citizens boycott Knesset elections for ideological reasons, but the majority are reluctant to take part in this political game because of the conduct of their parties,” said Arik Rudnitzky, from the Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem.
This trend was defied in the latest election. “I believe the number one motivator specifically in these elections is fear. Fear of another term of the Netanyahu government or a right-wing government because Arab citizens have had enough in the past four years,” Mr. Rudnitzky told The Hindu.
This surge was used by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition to mobilise right-wing voters. Mr. Netanyahu, on his X, called on his supporters to vote for Likud and described the situation as a “matter of life and death”.
His posts tried to mobilise voters by calling the situation “a war at home.” This attempt was criticised by Arab parties for being racist and for inciting hatred.
A survey by the Israel Democracy Institute published in September revealed that a party’s position regarding foreign affairs and security, followed by the economy and high cost of living, were the two most influential factors determining the support of Jewish Israelis.
In contrast, more than half of the surveyed Arabs felt that the party’s position regarding crime in Arab society was one of the most important factors determining their vote.
A large voter turnout among Israeli Arabs is expected to benefit the Arab parties, thereby improving the chances of Arab representation in the Knesset committees and better policies or support for them. This is evident in the exit polls and latest numbers which have put Arab parties leading in at least 17 seats in the Knesset
However, it is also true that not all Arab citizens support Arab parties. “In general, approximately 15% of the Arab or Arab citizens support non-Arab parties, Jewish parties. Most of them support  centrist parties. Also the Democrats headed by Yair Golan enjoy relative significant support in the Arab sector,” said Mr. Rudnitzky.
Latest numbers also show that neither the Netanyahu-bloc nor the Opposition coalition is set to secure a clear majority, meaning that Arab parties could hold the key as to who forms the government this time.

articles.title_orig: It's OK, Pokémon And Retro Gaming Fans, The Resellers And Vultures Will Eventually Move On
articles.title_zh: It's OK, Pokémon And Retro Gaming Fans, The Resellers And Vultures Will Eventually Move On
articles.content_orig:
An Inside Baseball Week dive into the sneaker market, the canary in the coalmine for these speculative vultures
If you're a fan of stuff like Pokémon cards or old video games and have been distraught at the state of things in 2026 , with resellers and middlemen wedging themselves into the market and destroying the affordability of what used to be a fun little hobby, I think there's value in considering a future where this doesn't happen anymore.
I'm not saying this as someone struck down by a debilitating and possibly terminal case of optimism. I'm saying it as someone who has seen this all before, elsewhere, and has seen how the gas eventually ran out of the speculative boom that attracted the parasites in the first place, and where things have now returned to some semblance of normality: sneakers.
I spent almost a decade, through the 2010s and into Covid, as someone who landed somewhere between "enthusiast" and "collector" on the sneakerhead scale . I've always been into shoes--I remember asking for a pair of Jordan VI Infareds for Christmas in sixth grade, and being politely told by my parents to get in the bin--but after finally growing old enough to have some disposable income, much of my 30s was spent following, talking about and buying sneakers.
Some of my favourite pairs from my collecting days
It was a lot of fun for a while there, but things started to go downhill once people from outside of sneakers caught wind of how much money was being made buying and reselling shoes. As soon as you start seeing mainstream news reports about long lines for products , limited supply, immense demand and the resulting stratospheric resale prices (as we did in the 2010s with Yeezys, Ultraboosts, NMDs and Jordan/Dunk re-releases), those products stop being 'grails' for the fans, and start becoming commodities anyone could invest in.
Nearing the end of the 2010s, manufacturers like Nike and Adidas leaned into the hype cycles created by releasing their most sought-after shoes in limited quantities. Massive online commerce platforms like StockX and GOAT grew their businesses, and what had once been an enthusiast market had been overrun by speculators and investors . A common sight on social media around this time would be photos of rooms, and sometimes even warehouses , full of sneaker boxes, as unscrupulous resellers worked out ways to engineer online auctions and retail releases to secure huge quantities of shoes that might have retailed for $150, but could be resold for over $300.
This caused enormous frustration among sneakerheads, in the same way it's causing frustration for long-time Pokémon players and retro gaming collectors now. There was literally no need for this vampiric class of middlemen to have inserted themselves between fans and their intended purchase! Manufacturers could have sold those products directly to people who actually wanted them!
Nothing lasts forever though. In 2018 the sneaker market seemed like a new frontier in consumerist money-printing, a bottomless well of demand and resale inflation, but just a few years later Yeezy had crashed and burned as a brand, Ultraboosts had run out of steam and Nike had become so reliant on milking classic silhouettes like Jordans and Dunks that it started sinking the entire company . Brands like Adidas moved away from rapper collabs and started reinvesting in performance athletic shoes, which can be bought at any store you walk into, and companies like Hoka, Salomon and On, once existing on the fringes of the sneaker market, have capitalised on a boom in running, trails and fashion trends like gorpcore to grow into major players, helping sink demand for traditional "hyped" shoes as they've ascended .
Companies like StockX remain, and there are still hyped sneaker releases, but the scene in 2026 is nothing like it was in 2016. If you want a pair of new shoes now, there's a good chance you can just jump online and get them directly from a manufacturer or specialist store. Personally I've only bought two pairs of shoes at resale since Covid: one pair on StockX at half its retail price that the seller must have accepted just to get rid of their stock, and another on Depop at retail from a guy who bought the wrong size from a running store that didn't accept returns. That's a far cry from 2016-2020, when I was camped out in Discords and subreddits, entering raffles and sharing tips on how to secure sought-after pairs.
Anyway, that brief recap is my way of not just setting the scene for the rise and fall of sneaker resale's golden age, but also to really help fans of stuff like TCGs and classic Nintendo games through their own suffering. I'm not really a sneaker journalist though, so for Inside Baseball Week I spoke with Russ Bengtson, former editor-in-chief of SLAM magazine, long-time sneaker editor at Complex and, disclaimer, author of a tome ( A History Of Basketball In 15 Sneakers ) that sits proudly on my living room bookshelf.
Luke Plunkett: Hey man, thanks for chatting with us. I've already given readers a very brief recap on the ups and downs of sneaker resale, but what do you think caused a decline in the importance of resellers in the market? Do you think it was saturation, complacency from Nike, something else, maybe all of the above?
Russ Bengtson : I think it's all of the above, and on top of that it was never something that was going to last at that level forever to begin with. You had something of a perfect storm of models—Nike in particular—from roughly 1985 to 2001, '82 if you count the Air Force 1, that were lightning in a bottle from design to marketing, that had a second life once those of us who were teens in that two-decade or so span got jobs and got money and were able to buy all the stuff we either wanted or had as kids. We had first-hand experience with and connections to all of those shoes.
As we get further away from that era, those who really wanted them are aging out and probably already have everything they wanted, and the next generation only experienced those shoes as retros. The marketing, to steal from Fight Club , becomes a copy of a copy of a copy. And then on top of that, yes, resale hubs and personal resellers already have so many pairs of all the "grail" shoes—every re-retro becomes less important—and Nike flooded the zone with so many releases that they lost their importance that way too.
LP: I guess I should be specific and accurate here: Is sneaker resale even dead? Companies like StockX keep reporting massive profits , but culturally--however you'd like to define that--it definitely seems like hyped launches and resale frenzies have dried up massively. What do you make of that discrepancy?
RB: I'm not sure it will ever be fully dead. There are obviously some shoes that still fetch absurd prices—thinking of some original '85 Jordan 1s and a lot of the more limited Dunk SBs that haven't been retroed yet. And then you have people paying resale for brands like Saucony and Brooks who weren't really in that conversation before, but now they too are doing the limited collaboration thing. And on top of that, I'm sure some people are just conditioned to buy through Stadium Goods or Flight Club or even eBay, and even on below retail sales they still get their cut. I'm not sure you're going to get as much of the "buy a whole store's allocation to drop off at a resale shop," but there will still be a resale market.
LP: Do you think, culturally at least, sneakers are in a healthier place now that the boom market has seemingly cooled?
RB: I have mixed feelings on this, and honestly on retro in general. I wrote a whole book that sought to put some of the more significant basketball sneakers into some kind of context, and what you have with retro is more or less complete context collapse. Back when retro was new and relatively rare, you had things like retro cards and even a burgeoning sneaker media trying to stay on top of things, but now it feels like it's just everything

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu claims stolen election amid failure to secure victory
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu claims stolen election amid failure to secure victory
articles.content_orig:
Print in a simple, ad-free format
Ad-free and in a comfortable reading format
Palestinian turnout in East Jerusalem in Tuesday's Knesset election broke all records since Israel annexed the eastern part of the city in 1967, as more than 10,000 residents exercised their right to vote – with the vast majority backing the Joint List – tripling the rate recorded in the previous election.
The overwhelming majority of the roughly 391,000 Palestinian residents of East Jerusalem are ineligible to vote in Knesset elections. After annexing the city, Israel refrained from granting them full citizenship, instead giving them "permanent resident" status, which grants the right to vote in municipal elections but not national ones.
Despite this, several thousand have obtained Israeli citizenship over the years. Estimates suggest that between 5 and 7 percent of East Jerusalem residents are now citizens and are included in the Knesset voter registry.
The election for the 26th Knesset on Tuesday brought no resolution.
The results may actually herald a period of political paralysis. For now, it's hard to discern a path that enables a rapid formation of a new government. Such a situation is better for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was worried about a rout, more than it favors his rivals in the "bloc of change."
But despite the impression he is trying to create through his loyalists in the media, the prime minister did not win this election. He did what Hezbollah tried to do for years in its clashes with Israel. Merely avoiding a loss is a win for Netanyahu.
A situation in which all sides fail to form a government, necessitating a caretaker government and another election, would be bad for Israel but not necessarily bad for Netanyahu. He gets to continue to be prime minister for now, and another election serves him since it's likely that his rivals have exhausted their electoral capabilities in the present round.
After counting most of the ballots, excluding absentee votes, it appears the opposition stands at about 67 Knesset seats in total, of which about 19 are for the Arab parties and about 48 for the Eisenkot bloc.
The coalition, however, currently has about 53 Knesset seats. So while Likud is the largest party with about 26 Knesset seats, the majority of the Israeli public clearly voted against the current government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. This government has lost substantial support since the last round of elections.
The figures clearly point to an unprecedented achievement by the Arab community, which voted en masse for political partnership with Jews. Despite the challenges and reservations about voting, and amidst a particularly racist incitement campaign, a record 19 Knesset seats loudly and clearly declare: We are an inseparable part of this country.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could remain in power despite his bloc falling short of a majority in Tuesday's election – a prospect that poses a dilemma for Israel's liberal supporters in the United States, who have long argued that Netanyahu does not represent Israel as a whole.
The contrast with Brazil, Hungary and Serbia, where voters have rejected leaders with authoritarian records, is stark. The Jewish-led 'bloc of change' in Israel could secure a parliamentary majority with the backing of Arab lawmakers. But key opposition leaders have ruled out relying on that support to replace Netanyahu.
Hadar Susskind, director of New Jewish Narrative, said that if the opposition boycotts the Arab parties, its standing will continue to plummet among Democrats in the U.S.
"If you're a progressive member of Congress who cares about Israel and does not support Netanyahu and you've heard for so many years that ' Netanyahu is not Israel ' and that it's a democracy," Susskind said, "and then you see that the opposition has 67 seats and can form a government, but they won't do it – what's the problem?"
With 90.4 percent of the votes counted, the Netanyahu bloc remains at 53 seats and the opposition at 67, including 48 for Eisenkot's bloc and 19 for the Arab-majority parties.
The Central Elections Committee said it began counting absentee votes, known in Israel as "double envelopes," at 1 A.M.
With 89.8 percent of ballots counted, the Netanyahu bloc remains at 53 seats and the opposition at 67: The Arab-majority parties with 19 and the bloc led by opposition frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot at 48, according to the Central Elections Committee.
The committee said 11,687 out of 12,018 standard polling stations have been processed, while the remainder are undergoing routine verification processes standard for every election campaign.
Hundreds of Israeli writers, artists and creators, including globally renowned actor Itay Tiran and singer Achinoam Nini, joined a petition Wednesday calling on opposition bloc leaders to "join forces in a bold, groundbreaking and historic act" in light of the emerging election results, and to "stop the chaos from continuing under the ultra-far-right-wing government and Netanyahu."
In the full petition , the signatories write: "We, writers and poets, theater professionals, multidisciplinary artists and cultural journalists, call on the entire Change Bloc, across its Jewish and Arab factions, to unite as a single alliance and join together in a bold, groundbreaking and historic act to create a better, more equal, tolerant and shared reality."
"We ask that you rise above the prejudice, racism and incitement to which we have become accustomed."
"The Arab parties are extending a hand to repair the damage, and we must not ignore that outstretched hand," they added.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot issued his first response since his speech on Tuesday, saying he was focused on forming what he called a "Zionist government of enlistment" and bringing change to Israel.
"This is the people's will, having expressed no confidence in the October 7 government and its draft-dodging, and in the draft-dodging bloc as a whole," Eisenkot wrote on X.
Welcome to the day after Israel's election, where a 56 percent parliamentary majority is a crushing defeat and a 44 percent minority is a landslide victory.
That is, if you accept the narrative Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spent years entrenching in Israeli society: that a government backed by Arab votes is illegitimate. It was the premise of the most racist and Islamophobic election campaign in Israel's history.
Around 24 hours after the polls closed, with most votes counted, the projected results should signal a decisive victory for those seeking to unseat Netanyahu: 67 of the Knesset's 120 seats, against just 53 for his bloc. There is only one problem: Some 730,000 people, at least, voted for Arab parties, giving them an estimated 19 seats – nearly 16 percent of parliament.

Apple has officially entered the touchscreen MacBook Pro era, and apparently, it wants to drain your wallet while it’s at it.
The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, which is already a hefty price tag in this economy. But if you want the absolute top-of-the-line model with every possible upgrade, prepare to cough up around $14,549.
As MacRumors first reported, Apple’s configurator prices the fully loaded 14-inch model at $14,249 and the 16-inch version at $14,549. Both come equipped with Apple’s top-tier M5 Max chip, featuring an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU.
You can blame the ongoing memory shortage and AI’s seemingly endless appetite for hardware for some of the pricing pressure. Moving to a 4TB SSD costs an additional $1,000, while upgrading to 8TB adds $3,000. Want the new 16TB option? That’ll set you back another $7,000.
Another $2,000 gets you 128GB of memory, while nano-texture glass adds $150.
For some perspective, the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro topped out at $10,149. The new model raises that ceiling by a whopping $4,400.
Absurd prices aside, the launch marks a significant shift for Apple, nearly a decade after it first experimented with the Touch Bar . The company eventually abandoned that feature, but now it’s ready to embrace a touchscreen MacBook Pro.
Preorders open October 30, with availability beginning November 6.

articles.title_orig: What Robinhood's CFO found interesting about Anthropic's IPO prospectus
articles.title_zh: What Robinhood's CFO found interesting about Anthropic's IPO prospectus
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Seemingly, everyone is digging into Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO prospectus this week, even other C-suite execs like Robinhood ( HOOD ) CFO Shiv Verma.
"I have gone through it. The growth rates are pretty incredible, … up 1,300% year over year, I can't recall seeing another company doing that well," Verma said on Yahoo Finance about what caught his attention from the prospectus.
"The other thing I thought was interesting is they were showing what percentage of their customers are in different buckets," Verma added. "And so if you spend more than $10 million a year, you're a top 250 customer. I thought that was a pretty interesting stat, as I thought it'd be a little bit larger, but it just goes to show you how big their future TAM [total addressable market] is."
Verma has no choice but to read every single page of the S-1 for at least two reasons.
For one, Verma runs point on Robinhood Ventures.
It's a concentrated investment portfolio heavily anchored in premier AI and data infrastructure giants, including OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), Databricks ( DATB.PVT ), the AI-hiring platform Mercor, and the coding assistant Cognition. So how Anthropic is received by investors could greatly impact the valuations of the companies in the portfolio and, by extension, the overall value of Robinhood.
Secondly, there will likely be a lot of interest from Robinhood's retail investor base, enthralled with all things AI, in trading Anthropic shares and also to use the hotly anticipated debut to scale in and out of other AI names.
As it stands, the S-1 has been generally well received by markets.
Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus showed. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.
On an adjusted basis, Anthropic posted $1.62 billion in operating income through the first six months of 2026 compared to a loss of $1.85 billion last year.
The company is winning praise for its strong top-line growth rates and more than $131 billion in cash on hand.
Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.
Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November. It plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
