articles.title_orig: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland
articles.title_zh: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland
articles.content_orig:
The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States.
The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia.
“It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,” Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it’s being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.”
The project has gained official support after repeated Trump administration attempts to claim Greenland were finally settled through a trilateral security agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark in September 2026. The agreement preserves Greenland’s autonomous territory status within the Kingdom of Denmark while expanding US military access. But relations have grown increasingly strained between the United States and its allies in Europe and Canada since President Trump initiated trade wars with multiple countries and has taken an increasingly pro-Russia stance on the war in Ukraine .
Europe has also been eyeing new Internet cable routes to Asia because more than 90 percent of communications between Europe and Asia run through undersea cables in the Red Sea, according to TeleGeography . Maintaining such cables has become riskier since open warfare resumed between the Yemeni government and Houthi faction this year, with Houthi forces having fired missiles and drones at commercial ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait chokepoint and the broader Red Sea.
The Pan-Arctic Cable took shape when European companies and research organizations joined forces with a Greenland telecom operator to sign an agreement on developing the project in 2025, according to Submarine Cable Networks.
Since that time, the project has received European Union backing through the Connecting Europe Facility Digital program. The European Union has already invested $119 million (107 million euros) to “advance Greenland’s secure and sovereign connectivity” along with funding the Pan-Arctic Cable plan, according to the new European Commission policy document on Europe’s Arctic strategy.
But the goal of eventually extending the undersea cable to Japan and South Korea by way of Canada faces considerable challenges, including requiring more European icebreaker ships to support the installation and maintenance of the cable in icy Arctic waters. Multiple pan-Arctic projects have been proposed in the past and some are still in development.
One earlier project known as the Arctic Connect subsea cable aimed to connect Europe and Asia using the Northern Sea Route running along Russia’s Arctic coastline—but that was eventually halted in May 2021 before the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine led to growing Russian isolation from Europe.
Still, the Pan-Arctic Cable is not the only subsea cable project that could strengthen Europe’s ties to friendlier nations. In September 2026, the Norwegian company Bulk Infrastructure Group AS began looking for a Canadian partner to take a majority ownership stake in a new transatlantic cable directly linking Europe to Canada, according to Bloomberg News . That proposed project has been named the Leif Erikson system.
In previous decades, “geopolitics played virtually no role when companies considered where to put their cables and what countries to connect,” said Braw, whose book Undersea War explores why the world has become more dangerous for the Internet’s undersea backbone . But the focus on maximizing data connectivity and Internet traffic has given way to more complex planning that also accounts for international relations and the growing risk of adversaries carrying out surveillance or sabotage of cables.
“We are going to see more cables that connect friendly countries, and then you have to figure out how you can connect friendly countries without going through unfriendly countries’ exclusive economic zones or territorial waters,” Braw told Ars.
Growing international tensions have coincided with suspicious incidents of Russian- and Chinese-linked commercial ships severing European undersea cables in the Baltic Sea by dragging their anchors for long periods of time. In spring 2026, NATO countries’ forces also confronted Russian submarines that were practicing how to disable undersea cables in Arctic waters near Norway, Reuters reported .
Europe’s new Arctic strategy document addresses such security threats by stating that the European Union will establish an Arctic Cable Hub to “monitor, protect and support the repair of submarine cables in the North Atlantic-Arctic.” It also says the European Union will invest in “smart technologies on cables that act as early warning systems for potential threats.”
Such risks for undersea infrastructure are not limited to the Baltic Sea or Atlantic Ocean. In the Pacific Ocean, Chinese-linked commercial ships have also severed undersea cables near Taiwan. Analysts have documented Chinese research vessels spending unusual amounts of time near Pacific undersea cables and warned of the rising risks for US-linked subsea cable projects that are often owned by Big Tech companies such as Google and Meta .
Meanwhile, Iran has threatened to charge fees to subsea cable operators whose cables run through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint. That action comes as part of a broader regional war in the Middle East that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026—and Iran has drawn up plans to potentially attack undersea cables if hostilities ramp up once again.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft's cloud growth, cash flow offer respite from AI spending fears
articles.title_zh: Microsoft's cloud growth, cash flow offer respite from AI spending fears
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Two tech behemoths -- Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) -- reported earnings today. Both showed strong cloud growth, but the market is treating them very differently. Microsoft shares popped after hours while Alphabet stock sank. Why?
I think a big part of the answer is how each plans to pay for the massive outlays both have planned.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Microsoft beat Wall Street's targets with sales up 19%, reaching $92.3 billion. GAAP -- generally accepted accounting principles -- earnings per share (EPS) came in at $4.92. Adjusted EPS was $4.89, above the roughly $4.72 the Street expected. Azure, its cloud platform, grew 48%, reaching $33.17 billion in revenue.
Alphabet's cloud growth was even stronger than Microsoft's: 103% growth for the unit, earning $11.1 billion in operating income on $30.7 billion in sales. Overall, sales jumped 25%, reaching $127.6 billion, slightly missing estimates, while GAAP EPS actually fell from $2.87 to $2.12. Search and YouTube ads also underperformed.
Some of Alphabet's EPS drop can be explained by an $8.7 billion net loss on equity securities, but even if you remove this -- worth $0.55 per share -- the earnings still came in well below what Wall Street was looking for.
While it's not a great look, I think the real issue the market is reacting to is the company's cash picture. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures (capex), up from $24.0 billion a year ago. Operating cash flow -- the cash the actual business generated -- was $42.3 billion. That left free cash flow (FCF) -- the money left after paying for its capex investments -- at negative $9.1 billion. That's worse than the negative $5.9 billion the company reported last quarter.
During the quarter, Alphabet raised $28.7 billion through senior unsecured notes and $12.4 billion from selling stock. Long-term debt has grown from $46.5 billion at the end of 2025 to $125.1 billion.
Alphabet said its capex guidance for 2026 holds -- $195 billion to $205 billion -- but said it expects capex in 2027 to "increase significantly."
Microsoft, on the other hand, is still FCF positive, though like Alphabet, that figure is moving in the wrong direction. The company reported FCF of $18.63 billion, down 27% year over year, after $39.37 billion in cash capital spending. Its broader capex figure, which includes finance leases, was $45.2 billion.
CFO Amy Hood said on July's earnings call that the company expects to stay free-cash-flow positive for its current fiscal year, though capex is expected to expand. On that call, she also said demand for its cloud services was running ahead of supply.
Microsoft at this point has a much healthier cushion in its quarterly cash flow -- more room to keep spending while it waits for those investments to pay off. Alphabet is increasingly asking lenders and shareholders to help cover the bill.
Obviously, the growth is hard to argue with, but I still think the jury is out on whether this bet will pay off for both companies. Costs are climbing, and I'm concerned the math won't pencil out long term.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration will allow pharmacies to make popular peptides
articles.title_zh: Trump administration will allow pharmacies to make popular peptides
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides. A new policy will make it easier for small compounding pharmacies to make them. Heather Diehl/Getty Images hide caption
Unproven but popular peptides touted for wellness have been available on the gray market, despite an official ban. Now, the Department of Health and Human Services is looking to bring them out of the shadows.
HHS said in a new policy that it will exercise enforcement discretion for a half dozen peptides, essentially looking the other way when they're made by small compounding pharmacies.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been a vocal supporter of peptides , saying he has used some of them himself.
Peptides are strings of amino acids, shorter than proteins, that can exert powerful effects in the body. Some occur naturally and others are synthetic variations. Wellness influencers and some clinicians have promoted unproven peptides for a wide range of uses, though the evidence for their safety and effectiveness is sparse.
So even though these peptides have not been through the Food and Drug Administration's rigorous drug review and approval process, they could become easier to get. But the policy's focus on smaller producers may mean that pharmacists will have a tough time meeting demand.
In July, a panel of advisers to the FDA voted in favor of expanded access to six peptides through compounding pharmacies. However, at the same meeting the FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the existing restrictions on them.
The new policy says compounding is a safer alternative to illicit "research-use-only" peptides that are available online. They're often sourced from sketchy suppliers overseas.
The peptides, and some of their unproven uses, are:
Joshua Fritzler, the president of Olympia and Wesley Pharmaceuticals in central Florida, says people have been asking about these peptides for years. But because they were illegal to compound, his company didn't make them.
The new policy doesn't change their legal status, but it does create a path for small compounders, called 503A compounding pharmacies. It doesn't apply to the larger ones, called 503Bs, that are outsourcing facilities producing higher volumes of medicines.
So at Fritzler's company, only its smaller compounding facility will be able to make the peptides – and only in small quantities, he says.
And that has implications for consumers.
"We won't be able to meet demand," he says, explaining that Olympia will likely only compound one of the six peptides and needs to get its facility ready first. "I don't think all the [503]As in the country could meet the demand."
The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding's CEO Scott Brunner wrote in a statement that his group is pleased with the administration's decision to allow the peptides to be compounded because it offers a "more accountable alternative" for patients seeking gray market peptides.
"It also brings patients into a system where pharmacy standards, regulatory oversight, and serious adverse event reporting apply," he says.
Brunner warned, however, that it may take some time for compounding pharmacies to begin dispensing these products to patients. That's because ingredient suppliers need to make sure their active ingredients meet the policy's requirements — and pharmacies need to verify that, too.
Several consumer advocacy groups say the policy puts patients at risk, however. The nonprofit Public Citizen noted that Kennedy seems to have acted unilaterally rather than through the typical rulemaking process.
"By allowing unproven and potentially unsafe peptides to be manufactured, marketed and prescribed without concern about potential federal enforcement actions, Kennedy has undermined the FDA and threatened public health," Dr. Robert Steinbrook, Health Research Group Director at Public Citizen wrote in a statement. "All peptide substances should go through the standard FDA approval process for new drugs. The HHS Secretary should support, not sabotage, needed FDA enforcement actions to protect consumers."
Steinbrook advised clinicians to talk to their patients and tell them about the risk of contamination and other adverse effects.
The Partnership for Safe Medicines, which includes various pharmacy and pharmacist organizations around the country, filed a citizen petition last week, urging the FDA to ignore the recommendation from its advisory committee in July to allow compounding pharmacies to make the six peptides.
"Today's decision leaves Americans in a grey area as to whether peptides are safe or not, even though the FDA's own scientists recommended against voting in favor of these substances due to concerns with evidence," its executive director Shabbir Safda wrote in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Weil, Gotshal & Manges, longtime Wall Street law firm, plans wind down
articles.title_zh: Weil, Gotshal & Manges, longtime Wall Street law firm, plans wind down
articles.content_orig:
A management committee of Weil, Gotshal & Manges , the long-time Wall Street law firm, has recommended that its partners wind down operations, the firm said Wednesday.
The recommendation came after an exodus of partners and the reported end, days ago, of talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher about a potential merger.
Weil, which has about 1,200 lawyers, in 2025 reportedly had more than $2 billion in revenue across multi-national operations.
"For more than 90 years, Weil, Gotshal & Manges has had the privilege of advising clients on some of their most consequential matters," the firm said in a statement to CNBC.
"Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm's Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down," the firm said. "The partners are expected to vote in the coming days."
Weil said that during the wind-down process in coming months, the "firm will continue serving clients with the dedication and excellence that have defined it since its founding and will remain committed to supporting its colleagues."
Over the years, Weil had been involved in major bankruptcy filings, including for Lehman Brothers, General Motors and Enron.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu rivals weigh joining forces with Arab parties
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu rivals weigh joining forces with Arab parties
articles.content_orig:
Isabel Kershner Johnatan Reiss Aaron Boxerman Qasim Nauman and Leo Sands
Israel’s political leaders were bracing for weeks of negotiations over a new government, as initial results on Wednesday showed no clear winner in a tightly fought election that many have described as a make-or-break moment for the country.
By Wednesday evening in Israel, election officials had counted about 90 percent of the ballots. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hard-line bloc of parties held a modest lead in seats over the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, but it appears that neither coalition will win the 61 seats needed to secure a straightforward majority in the Knesset, Israel’s Parliament.
That means both leaders would need to find support from outside their coalitions to form a government. Two Arab parties were on track to win as many as 19 seats, a strong showing that potentially gives them an important role in the negotiations, even though most Jewish parties were not eager to enter an alliance with them.
Some of Mr. Netanyahu’s allies have floated the idea that he could join Mr. Eisenkot and other centrists to form a broad unity government to stay in power. For Mr. Netanyahu, who will remain a caretaker prime minister until a government is formed, that would be a comfortable scenario.
Mr. Eisenkot faces a dilemma. He has denounced Mr. Netanyahu as unfit to lead Israel, but he has also objected to partnering with Arab parties in a potential coalition. On Wednesday, Mr. Eisenkot did not explicitly mention the Arab parties but said he was focused on forming a government that was both Zionist and committed to universal military conscription, a message that rules out alliances with both Arab and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
The Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties that has emerged as a potential kingmaker according to preliminary results, said it would “do everything in its power” to remove Mr. Netanyahu from office. That could signal a willingness to back Mr. Eisenkot’s bid to form an anti-Netanyahu coalition, even if its lawmakers have not been invited to join it.
The final tally of votes is not expected to be finished before Thursday evening. Lengthy negotiations are likely to follow as political parties try to assemble a governing majority. If those talks fail, the country could head to a second round of elections — a scenario that has played out before.
Here’s what else we are covering:
Vote count: The nearly 90 percent of votes counted indicate that Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition will receive about 54 seats, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc will get roughly 49, and the Arab parties could reach as many as 19. But the numbers could still shift.
Parliamentary control: Even if no government is formed, the Israeli Parliament will open on Nov. 10, and Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents could be well-placed to take control of the legislative process. Read more ›
Herzog’s role: President Isaac Herzog of Israel holds a largely ceremonial position, except after national elections, when it falls to him to select who gets the first crack at forming a new government. Read more ›
What Israelis think: The day after Israel’s election, almost everyone in the country was asking the same question: What now? The Times spoke to people from across the political spectrum to get a sense of their hopes and fears. Read more ›
For decades, Israel’s Arab parties have been relegated to the margins of Israeli political life, often sitting on the sidelines while Jewish parties assembled a governing coalition in Parliament and picked a prime minister.
Heading into Israel’s pivotal election on Tuesday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned his supporters that the Arabs were “trying to steal the election,” though electoral officials said there were no reports of widespread irregularities. He repeatedly invoked the specter of Arab voters to galvanize his right-wing base, vowing to keep them out of power.
Mr. Netanyahu’s leading rival, Gadi Eisenkot, largely declined to answer whether he would partner with Arab parties if necessary to topple the Netanyahu government, though he said none met his conditions as potential allies.
But record turnout on Tuesday by supporters of the Arab parties looks to deliver them their largest vote totals in generations, possibly since Israel’s establishment 78 years ago.
Now, the Arab minority represents a political reality that cannot be ignored.
Turnout in the Arab community, which represents about 20 percent of Israeli citizens, appears to have translated into a stunning windfall of parliamentary seats — potentially as many as 19 combined between the two leading parties, Raam and the Joint List alliance. The Arab parties have 10 seats in the outgoing Parliament.
Israel’s future could turn in part on whether Mr. Eisenkot decides to take the political risks of partnering with them. Without their support, Mr. Eisenkot and his alliance will almost certainly fall short of the 61-seat majority required in the 120-seat Parliament to form a new government and end Mr. Netanyahu’s hold on power. Mr. Netanyahu’s alliance also looks to fall short of 61 seats.
Many Israeli Jews have long objected to building a governing coalition that relies on Arab party backing for a majority. Some say a Jewish state should be ruled exclusively by Jews. Some cite national security reasons, questioning whether Arab leaders who see themselves as part of the wider Palestinian people can be entrusted with crucial matters of state.
Those objections became even more acute after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and the subsequent rightward shift in Israeli politics. Both Raam and some members of the Joint List condemned the assault, although they have also been highly critical of how Israel has conducted its war against Hamas in Gaza.
The Arab parties for many years were themselves reluctant to join governments that oversaw the Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza. And turnout among Arab Israelis has traditionally been lower than Jewish turnout, reflecting doubts about their ability to influence national decision-making.
Raam, a socially conservative party with roots in Islamist politics, has achieved some acceptance in Israel’s mainstream by putting less emphasis on the cause of Palestinian statehood. But the Joint List, an alliance of three smaller parties that includes a joint Jewish-Arab leftist faction and a Palestinian nationalist faction, is seen as more antagonistic toward Zionism.
Initial election results show that the Joint List will be the significantly larger of the two in Parliament.
“Netanyahu knows that without the Arab parties, there’s no majority to unseat him. That’s why he incites against us,” said Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Joint List alliance in an interview. “The opposition should reject that incitement.”
He added: “The ball is now in Eisenkot’s court. Whoever wants to remove Netanyahu and change his policies — we are ready to cooperate to topple his government.”
Political analysts say the Joint List would be more likely to support Eisenkot from outside the governing coalition, for instance by agreeing to block any no-confidence votes. There is some precedent for this: In the 1990s, then Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin relied on Arab lawmakers to prevent the collapse of his own minority government.
Arab citizens, some of whom view themselves as both Israeli and Palestinian, experience a tension that can cut to the heart of daily life. Unlike Palestinians in the West Bank — who live under Israeli military rule — Arab Israelis can vote, and some have held high office, including on the country’s Supreme Court.
But they largely live in separate cities and towns from Jewish Israelis and retain tight familial and historical bonds with Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Many view themselves as second-class citizens in the Jewish state, saying they face discrimination in housing as well as neglect in receiving public services.

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.content_orig:
The horrific crash south of Madrid was caused by human error after a computer system failure, officials say
• Deadly rail crash: Scores of people have been killed and about 100 injured after a high-speed train collided with a stationary train south of Madrid. Spain’s transport minister called it “inexplicable” that a train was allowed to continue its journey despite a red signal being in place.
• ‘People were hurled into the air ’: Several witnesses told CNN about the chaotic moment when passengers were thrown airborne during the collision. Rescue operations are still ongoing and the high-speed line linking Madrid with Andalusia remains suspended.
• Third train crash this year: This is the third rail disaster in Spain in 2026. In January, two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz , in southern Spain’s Córdoba province, killing more than 40 people. A commuter train near Barcelona derailed days later.
• Lee nuestra cobertura en español
Our live coverage has ended. Read more about the deadly train crash here .
At least 68 people were killed and about 100 were injured after a high-speed train smashed into a stationary train in Spain on Wednesday.
Crews are now working with flood lights to search for anyone else trapped in the wreckage as investigators try to figure out what led to the tragedy.
What we know : A computer system failure led to an issue with the safety system along a 63-kilometer (40-mile) stretch of track between Madrid and Seville causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically, said Óscar Puente, the country’s transport minister.
Puente said Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, then took manual command of the system and allowed the high-speed Renfe train to continue southbound toward Seville despite a red light. That train later collided with the stationary Iryo train.
Response: More than 500 emergency personnel have been deployed to the site, the Spanish Interior Ministry said. The Civil Guard said investigators are using drones to create a 3D reconstruction of the area and determine the accident’s possible causes.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said authorities are working hard to identify the cause of the crash and vowed that any negligence, if identified, will be addressed with “utmost firmness.” This is the third rail incident in Spain this year.
CNN’s Billy Stockwell, Michael Rios, Pau Mosquera and Duarte Mendonca, Jennifer Hansler, Sophie Tanno and Sol Amaya contributed reporting to this post.
Police were seen clashing with protesters and far right groups in the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday night as crowds demanded the resignation of Spanish government officials following a deadly train crash that left at least 68 dead.
Around 500 demonstrators gathered outside the Transport Ministry, with some throwing bottles and flares at police, Reuters reported. Video showed police deploying tear gas in an attempt disperse the large group gathered.
Protesters held signs saying “Leave!” next to a picture of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, while others held signs saying “Criminals” and “Corruption kills.” Sanchez’s socialist PSOE party has suffered a series of setbacks and corruption scandals this year involving close associates that have tarnished its reputation.
Spanish trade union CSIF is demanding the resignation of Óscar Puente, the country’s transport minister, after he said an “inexplicable” erroneous order from a train controller resulted in Wednesday’s deadly crash .
While discussing the circumstances of the collision, Puente said a computer system failure led to an issue with the safety system along a 63-kilometer (40-mile) stretch of track causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically.
Puente said Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, then took manual command of the system and a decision was made to allow the high-speed Renfe train to continue southbound toward Seville despite a red light. That train later collided with the stationary Iryo train.
CSIF, an independent trade union and civil servants’ association, accused Puente of using a “hardworking person” as a scapegoat instead of “assuming his responsibilities.” The trade union also said it had warned in September of “excess hours in Adif’s working days.”
CNN has approached Spain’s transport ministry for comment.
CNN’s Lauren Kent contributed reporting.
Renfe, Spain’s state-owned national railway operator, announced it has suspended service Thursday between Madrid and the Andalusia region.
One of Renfe’s trains was involved in a deadly collision earlier today, which killed at least 68 people. The Renfe train plowed into a stationary train operated by the private company Iryo, at a time when all train traffic in the area was disrupted due to a problem with the LZB train management safety system.
The collision occurred on the route between Madrid and Seville and an alternative transportation plan will be provided on Friday, Renfe said.
The service suspension also applies to trains coming from Barcelona and Valencia to Seville and Malaga, Renfe said in a post on X .
Some of cars derailed and officials are still searching for anyone trapped in the rubble.
Ana has been searching for her husband, Pepe, all day. But so far, no luck.
She raced to Madrid as soon as she heard about Wednesday’s deadly train collision in the Spanish province of Toledo, she told Reuters. Pepe was traveling on the high-speed Renfe train that crashed into the stationary Ilyo train while heading from Madrid to Seville.
Ana, who only provided her first name, told Reuters that Pepe’s name was not on the list of victims who have been identified.
Local police did however find Ana’s dog, who had been traveling with Pepe.
“Poor thing, I think he’s had a bad time,” she told Reuters, speaking from a school in Urda – the town closest to the site of the train crash – where relatives have been advised to wait.
Renfe, a state-owned railway company, said it had opened a special phone line for families of victims, Reuters reported.
In the days ahead, investigators in Spain will continue to gather details to understand what exactly led to the deadly train collision that killed at least 68 people, said Janos Rozsa, a railway accident investigator and safety specialist.
Spain’s transport minister said the was crash caused by human error after a computer system failure, but Rozsa said “accidents rarely have a single cause.”
Incidents like this “usually result from a combination of different contributing factors that are present at the same time,” he told CNN’s Isa Soares.
Officials will use things like surveillance cameras and data recorders on the trains and on the signaling system to piece together how the trains were moving and how they ended up on the same piece of track.
While human error may be one part of the what caused the crash, it will also be important for investigators to fully understand “the circumstances in which people were working and how the overall system was designed to keep these trains apart.”
While this is the third rail disaster in Spain this year, Rozsa said it is too early to draw any conclusions if the incidents had any common threads.
Scores of people were killed after two trains collided in Spain on Wednesday, in a crash that authorities say was caused by both computer system failure and apparent human error.
Spain’s transportation minister Óscar Puente said that a computer system failure led to an issue with the safety system along a 63-kilometer (40-mile) stretch of track causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically.
At that point, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, ADIF, took manual command of the system and a decision was made to allow the high-speed Renfe train to continue southbound along the tracks despite a red light.

articles.title_orig: Girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German wildlife park
articles.title_zh: Girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German wildlife park
articles.content_orig:
An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park.
She was inside an enclosure at the Johannismühle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said.
They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".
The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured.
The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details.
The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx.
The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild.
It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit.
Johannismühle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama.
The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe.
A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.

articles.title_orig: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
articles.title_zh: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
articles.content_orig:
The King shook off royal formality and replaced it with some dance moves on the second day of his nine-day visit to the Caribbean.
Armed with a pair of maracas in the colours of the flag of the Bahamas, Charles joined a Junkanoo - a cultural event and carnival designed to celebrate island life.
Amidst the feathered headdresses and brightly coloured costumes in the afternoon Caribbean heat, the King, dressed in a suit and sunglasses, joined dancers at the front of parade to cheers from the crowd.
It was a lighter mood coming after the King's arrival on Tuesday where he delivered a speech acknowledging the pain of the slave trade, describing "the suffering of the past".
Speaking at an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth on Tuesday, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.
Charles began the second day of his trip by paying his respects to fallen members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force (RBDF).
The King, wearing a set of medals and sunglasses, spoke with servicemen and women before he laid a wreath at the Flamingo Monument, which commemorates four RBDF Marines killed when Cuban MiG fighter aircraft sunk HMBS Flamingo in May 1980.
Later, on a visit to the Bahamas Boxing Academy, the King found young fighters and the head coach wearing an image of himself emblazoned on club t-shirts showing the King complete with a crown, gloves and a boxing belt.
"He loved it, he loved it," said Jermaine Gibson, president of a neighbouring boxing club who wore one of the t-shirts. "He said it was really good and we gave him one of his own."
The King watched two young fighters sparring in the ring at the academy which trains boys and girls from the age of eight to 18 years old.
"I might see you at a Commonwealth Games," the King told a group of children at the boxing academy.
Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site was once a rubbish dump but has been redeveloped and now protects 1,235 acres of mangroves.
The King walked along a new boardwalk through the wetlands to see the conservation work being done to protect this vulnerable, low lying island from climate change.
He met students carrying out field work in the wetland waters asking them about their exams and ambitions to be marine biologists.
"We've so been looking forward to this," said Joanne Smith, president of the Bahamas National Trust Council.
"We want more Bahamians to get involved in our national parks so they can use it to better themselves… we are so pleased to have the King here, this is really significant for us."
Then it was on to the Junkanoo, where the King could be seen dancing alongside attendees dressed in feathered headdresses and bright costumes.
The history of the Junkanoo is not clear but it's believed it emerged out of the slave trade when enslaved men and women were given time off to mark Christmas.
A small protest near the parade, which had activists holding placards with the words "Pay us what you owe us", was moved on by the police.
The small group of protesters were from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.
The King acknowledged the "great suffering of the past" when he first arrived in the Bahamas, as he faced calls for slavery reparations.
Noelle Nicholls, chair of the reparations committee, said :"We are demanding an apology for those crimes, and reparations for the harm that was done."
Nicholls said the protesters' presence "amidst the pomp and pageantry of the celebrations... are for us also a sombre occasion, because this is the King returning in a way that has still not atoned for the sins of the past."
The King has confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery at a major summit in Antigua next week.
The King ended his day with a garden reception at Government House in Nassau where he met Bahamians who have made significant contributions to public life.
In a speech, Dame Cynthia A Pratt, the governor general of the Bahamas who is the King's representative on the island, described her pride at Charles visiting the country for the first time since 1973.
"We trust that your time in our capital will reflect the legendary hospitality of our people," said Dame Cynthia.
"We pray that this royal visit further strengthens the enduring bonds of friendship between the Crown and the Bahamian people."
On Thursday, the Caribbean tour leaves the Bahamas as the King continues his visit in Guyana.
The trip has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.
The King's engagements in Guyana will focus on the environment and biodiversity.
He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.
The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

articles.title_orig: All 16 D&D World of Warcraft Species Revealed
articles.title_zh: All 16 D&D World of Warcraft Species Revealed
articles.content_orig:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.
Over the past twenty years, the World of Warcraft MMORPG has introduced dozens of playable species. Now, many of these unique creatures and cultures are making the leap from the desktop to the tabletop courtesy of the upcoming D&D WoW crossover.
In total there are 16 new D&D WoW species. Five of these (Dwarf, Elf, Goblin, Human and Orc) are adaptations of existing D&D 5.5E species, while 11 of them (Dracthyr, Draenei, Earthen, Forsaken, Gnome, Haranir, Pandaren, Tauren, Troll, Vulpera and Worgen) are completely native to the world of Azeroth and appearing in 5.5E for the first time.
To help make sense of it all, we’ve put together this detailed species guide, which includes a high-level explanation of what the species is all about, along with their key traits within the D&D 5.5E ruleset. One important thing to note is that we have also included notes on Renown , which is an optional rule in the 2024 Dungeon Master’s Guide but is a major part of the new D&D Warcraft supplement. Each species has a base Renown score that determines how you interact with Azeroth’s many factions and offers in-game benefits such as access to magic items, discounts on equipment and new Bastion facilities.
With that in mind, below is a complete breakdown of all 16 species from the D&D WoW supplement. You can check them out for yourself, when the book arrives at your local game store, D&D Beyond and Amazon.
Dracthyr are draconic humanoids (somewhat similar to D&D’s Dragonborn ) who were created thousands of years ago by Neltharion , a god-like demon-dragon and leader of the black dragonflight (one of Azeroth’s five great families of dragons, each of which is tasked with protecting one particular aspect of the world). Neltharion combined the power of dragons with the adaptability of the mortal races to create what he believed would be an army of elite soldiers. Unfortunately, Neltharion was corrupted and driven mad by the Old Gods and became the villainous being known as Deathwing. As a result, his army off dracthyr was sealed away in stasis, sleeping for ten thousand years until they were eventually awakened in the Dragon Isles.
In their natural form, dracthyr are winged, scaled warriors, but can transform into a humanoid form known as a visage. In the World of Warcraft MMORPG, dracthyr are the only species that can play the Evoker class (a mechanic that has carried over into the new D&D supplement). It’s also important to note that within the 5.5E rules, a dracthyr’s creature type is Dragon rather than Humanoid, which does matter when it comes to certain spells, abilities and magic items.
Dracthyr are organized into military divisions called weyrns . When you create a dracthyr, you choose which weyrn you belong to. There are five options in the new D&D WoW supplement:
If you choose the Dark Talons (Horde) or the Obsidian Warders (Alliance), your Renown Score with that faction begins at 3. If you choose any other weyrn, your Renown Score with the Valdrakken Accord (the alliance of dragonflights based in the city of Valdrakken) begins at 3.
As a Dracthyr, you have these special traits.
Draenei are tall, blue-skinned humanoids with hooves, tails and face tendrils, and are one of the few playable species not originally from Azeroth. Instead, they are the descendants of a species known as the Eredar, who once dwelled on the distant world of Argus. When the dark Titan Sargeras offered the Eredar unimaginable power, two of their leaders accepted and became unholy lords of the demonic horde known as the Burning Legion . The third leader, the prophet Velen, foresaw these dark events and fled from Argus with his followers, with the group guided by benevolent beings made of holy energy known as naaru .
The Eredar who travelled with Argus called themselves draenei (which meant “exiled ones” in their language) and spent thousands of years fleeing across the cosmos with the Burning Legion in pursuit. Eventually their dimensional ship, known as the Exodar, crash-landed on Azeroth, where they joined the Alliance.
When you create a Draenei, you choose one of four Eredar Lineages:
If you choose the Draenei or Lightforged lineage, your Renown Score with the Exodar (Alliance) begins at 3. Otherwise, you have no starting Renown Score.
As a Draenei, you have these special traits.
At first glance, Azeroth’s Dwarves will feel familiar to most D&D players and fans of fantasy fiction. They’re stout, stubborn and famous for their mining, stonework, engineering and love of weapons and good ale. Their origin, however, is unique to Warcraft. Dwarves descend from the Earthen, beings of living stone built by the Titans (the godlike cosmic beings who shaped Azeroth). When the Old God Yogg-Saron afflicted the earthen with the “curse of flesh,” many asked to be sealed away in hibernation until a cure could be found. Ages later, they awoke as flesh-and-blood dwarves, journeyed to the snowy mountains of Dun Morogh and carved out the great city of Ironforge.
For more than two thousand years, Ironforge prospered through trade with the human kingdoms to the north. Then, about two centuries before the orcs invaded Azeroth, tensions between its three most powerful clans erupted into a civil conflict called the War of the Three Hammers. The Bronzebeard clan won the war and drove its rivals out of the mountain. Today, those old wounds have largely healed, and Ironforge is governed by the Council of Three Hammers, which includes representatives from all three clans and is considered a founding pillar of the Alliance.
When you create a dwarf, you can choose which clan you hail from. There are four options:
Whichever clan you choose, your Renown Score with Ironforge (Alliance) begins at 3.
You have the Dwarf species traits from the 2024 Player’s Handbook.
As a Dwarf, you have these special traits.
Earthen are beings of living stone created eons ago by the god-like Titans using a great machine called the Forge of Wills and were designed to mine and carve out Azeroth’s caverns. Over time, many earthen fell victim to the “curse of flesh,” which was engineered by the Old God Yogg-Saron. These victims became the ancestors of today’s dwarves. Large populations of stone earthen survived, however, primarily on the continent of Khaz Algar, where a titan device called the Awakening Machine roused them from stasis. After the dwarf king Magni Bronzebeard restored the machine, newly awakened earthen were allowed to choose their own path rather than follow the titans’ ancient instructions, and many have since joined the Alliance or the Horde.
In appearance, earthen resemble stocky dwarves carved from stone and infused with Azerite, the crystallized lifeblood of Azeroth. Crystals jut from their bodies and mineral growths take the place of hair and beards. They don’t need to eat, but consuming certain minerals or precious stones can slightly alter their appearance.
As newly awakened free agents with no long-standing ties to either faction, Earthen have no starting Renown Score.
As an Earthen, you have these special traits.
Every Elf of Azeroth traces their roots to the night elves, who once ruled a world-spanning empire built around a lake of raw magical energy known as the Well of Eternity. Their rulers soon became obsessed with arcane magic, which drew the attention of the Burning Legion . The resulting War of the Ancients ended with the Great Sundering, a cataclysm that shattered Azeroth’s single continent into the landmasses that exist today. Ten thousand years of conflict have since splintered elven society into several distinct peoples, five of which are playable in the new D&D 5.5E supplement:
Your starting Renown Score depends on which elven people you hail from:

Fans have been datamining various Nintendo Switch 2 games over the past few days, and Mario Kart World is the latest to receive this treatment. After combing through the files, a number of interesting names have surfaced.
Rimea shared the discovery on social media, as first found by MondoMega. The following drivers are in a file that relates to the character weight stats:
In addition to the above, Spiny, who is known as Togezo in Japanese, is said to be listed as a driver in several files.

articles.title_orig: Here are five key takeaways from the Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference
articles.title_zh: Here are five key takeaways from the Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense.
And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets .
At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda.
The Wednesday meeting saw the Fed hold rates steady, but two dissenting governors wanted a hike.
Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons."
We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication.
"I don't believe in forward guidance," Warsh said on Wednesday. His remarks echoed his move earlier this year to end the years-long practice of offering forward guidance — removing an important signal for Wall Street and Main Street alike.
Warsh himself has not contributed a "dot" to the central bank's quarterly chart showing where individual policymakers expect short-term interest rates to go, and he doesn't plan to do so.
Now the Fed will also have fewer decisions to discuss.
Follow Hamza Shaban on X @hshaban .

articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Israel ’s election has ended in a deadlock as no party is on track for a majority of the Knesset , exit polls have suggested.
The stalemate comes after three years of war waged in Gaza , Lebanon and Iran , which have plunged the Middle East into turmoil.
The election is widely seen as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu , who is seeking another term after a combined 19 years in power .
But now, the jostling for power between parties to achieve a governing coalition and name the next prime minister could take weeks or even months.
There are 38 different parties contesting the election, but most will not get enough votes to secure one of the 120 seats in the Knesset.
Israeli elections are based on nationwide proportional representation. Citizens cast votes for a single party – not for individual candidates – and the party’s number of seats is determined by the proportion of the national vote it receives.
To actually enter the Knesset, a party must receive at least 3.25 per cent of the vote, or four seats.
Historically, no single party has won a majority, ​so governments are formed by a coalition. If no one manages to form a coalition with a 61-seat majority, citizens return to the ballot box.
Polls opened at 7am local time and closed at 10pm that night (8pm GMT). An exit poll by Israeli TV channels revealed the initial results, but the official, full results will not be confirmed until Tuesday 4 November.
However, the whole process will take much longer, ranging from 20 to 100 days. In the past two decades, no government has been sworn in in less than 50 days.
After a coalition agreement is signed, the Knesset convenes a special session during which the designated prime minister presents the new government and its policy agenda.
A formal vote is then held, and if the new government wins the vote, it starts its tenure.
The election is viewed domestically as one of the most consequential in the history of Israel .
The outcome could have profound consequences for Palestinians and Israel’s relations with neighbouring states, as well as international partners like the US and Europe.
Some of the main issues centre on the debate over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews , how the state should investigate its inability to prevent the October 7 2023 Hamas attacks and future concessions in Gaza , the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.
Israel’s wars have also put pressure on the economy, so the cost of living will definitely weigh on people’s minds when casting their votes. For context, the state’s defence budget has doubled since 2023.
Two main blocs – of nearly equal weight – are facing off against each other. One is an alliance of far-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, and the other camp is led by Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defence Forces.
The current exit polls released by major Israeli TV stations suggested that Netanyahu’s bloc won 50 seats, the opposition won 52-53 and Arab parties won 17-18.
Dr Nimrod Nir, of Agam Labs, said that “the real political drama will begin the morning after the election”.
“Israel’s election is not a single game, but a tournament – and election day is only the opening round,” he added.
“Our polling suggests that neither bloc is likely to secure a governing majority, leaving three possible outcomes: a unity government bringing Netanyahu together with more liberal parties, an alternative coalition backed by Arab parties, or yet another election.”

articles.title_orig: Microsoft expects 'very few people' to accept buyout, CFO says in internal memo
articles.title_zh: Microsoft expects 'very few people' to accept buyout, CFO says in internal memo
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft expects 3,000 or fewer employees to accept the buyout it offered this week to more than a quarter of its workforce, a spokesperson told Business Insider.
The point was reiterated on Wednesday by Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood, who wrote in an internal memo that employees have been questioning the rationale behind the buyout.
"I know there have been some questions on the rationale behind the voluntary exit offer that we announced this week," Hood wrote. "Our intent is to offer employees agency if they choose to leave the company on their own terms. We expect very few people to select this offer because of the growth opportunities here at Microsoft."
The memo statement was part of a quarterly earnings email Hood typically sends internally to employees every quarter when Microsoft discloses its financials.
These memos mostly repeat what the company reports publicly, but this time Hood went out of her way to address the buyout offer, which caused quite a stir across the tech industry this week.
Earlier this year, Microsoft offered a different retirement buyout. In that situation, about one-third of eligible employees took the offer, and that helped Microsoft cut fewer employees in subsequent layoffs.
This week's buyout is getting a lot less uptake, according to the company.
This afternoon, we announced our first-quarter financial results. We exceeded Wall Street expectations, growing revenue 19% and operating income 21%.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
With the start of FY27, we also made an important change to how we report our business. We announced that we changed our reporting structure for the first time in 12 years, moving from three segments to two: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. This change better reflects how we are running the business today — from how we build products and allocate resources to how we create value for customers across the connected layers of our platform. To give you a sense of the two segments, looking back to last fiscal year, Agents and Infra would have represented about 81% of our revenue while Devices and Consumer would have been 19%.
A few highlights from the quarter across our two new segments:
Thank you for everything you did to deliver a strong start to the year. In particular, I want to thank our engineering and capacity delivery teams who are working to help us deliver more capacity faster and with high reliability. These teams are also using the capacity we have more efficiently to create room for us to better meet customer demand for the Azure platform, which continues to exceed our supply.
I know there have been some questions on the rationale behind the voluntary exit offer that we announced this week. Our intent is to offer employees agency if they choose to leave the company on their own terms. We expect very few people to select this offer because of the growth opportunities here at Microsoft. We'll continue to provide a broad set of options for employees to learn, gain new skills, and advance their careers here.
We have tremendous opportunity ahead of us. To meet the moment, we are focused on delivering great products and solutions that help our customers to achieve their many goals — security, innovation, growth — to name a few. Thank you for keeping positive, value-creating outcomes for our customers at the top of the list.
To hear more details about the quarter and our outlook for Q2, you can join live today at 2:30PM Pacific Time, listen on-demand, or read the transcript on the Investor Relations website. Finally, mark your calendars for Microsoft Ignite, on November 17-20, where we'll show how our innovation across AI, cloud, data, security, and Copilot is coming together to help customers transform their businesses.

articles.title_orig: Fed leaves rates steady as governor Lisa Cook dissents
articles.title_zh: Fed leaves rates steady as governor Lisa Cook dissents
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike.
The Fed's benchmark rates remained in the 3.75% to 4% range , as widely expected. A rate hike in December, however, appears far more likely, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Here are the key takeaways from the Fed's statement and Fed Chairman Warsh's press conference:
Fed upgrades economy from "solid" to "strong": The FOMC updated the language in its statement, adding that "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right policy stance. This suggests the Fed is not in a hurry to ease inflation.
But "inflation remains elevated": Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation down to the 2% target. Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , the Fed has positioned itself to continue assessing data.
Warsh announces changes to the Fed's schedule : In 2027, one of the eight Fed meetings will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed's funds rate nor a policy statement. In 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy.
Warsh refutes the idea that the decision was politically inflected: Warsh stated that "politics played no role in the decision" — something that generated some discussion with the US midterm elections next week.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he doesn't agree that Fed rate hikes will have no impact on artificial intelligence, given the strong demand for AI and the high returns investors expect.
"I was skeptical of that view," Warsh said during a press conference. "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything."
Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, in a post last month on X , expressed skepticism that higher rates would reduce demand and investment in AI.
"What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near infinite ROI and the demand for compute will remain incalculable," Ackman wrote. "What if the old models don't apply to the current paradigm?"
Warsh pointed to how credit spreads for certain assets have widened since the Fed raised rates in September, and financial conditions have tightened as investors have differentiated between tech firms and other companies to invest.
"With respect to the new technology and this investment surge, do interest rates matter? I believe they do," said Warsh. "And I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy."
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pushed back Wednesday on any suggestion that next week's midterm elections had a role in the Fed's decision to keep interest rates steady . He also dodged multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office.
But it wasn't for a lack of trying from the assembled reporters.
"I appreciate the question, but I'm not going to be responding to quotes from public officials," Warsh said during a press conference when presented with criticisms from President Trump that interest rates should be lower and that his colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee were "political."
When the subject turned to the midterm elections, Warsh was similarly curt.
"Politics played no role in the decision," the chair said, adding, "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense.
And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets .
At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda.
Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons."
We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication.
Wall Street can't make up its mind about the Fed.
Stocks dipped after the 2 p.m. statement, rallied as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke, then gave much of that back. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is holding a small gain, and chip stocks are doing most of the lifting.
The typical stock isn't doing as well. The equal-weighted S&P 500, which gives every company the same weight, is in the red. So are small caps.
The bond market is clearer about what it thinks. The 30-year Treasury yield is near its high of the day, and the 10-year yield is back above 5%. Higher long-term rates make borrowing more expensive for companies and homebuyers.
The dollar moved the other way and slipped against the euro during the press conference.
That leaves the streak. The S&P 500 came into Wednesday down on six straight Fed days, the second-longest run since 1994, which we pointed out at 2:43 p.m. ET. A higher close would end it, and a lower one would tie the 2018 record of seven.
Chairman Warsh said a couple of words on the Fed's independence amid some discussion that the US midterm elections — just six days away — and the perception that the Fed could influence them could sway the Fed's decision.
"Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh stated. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
"But I will say," Warsh added, "it's an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do with politics."
The Fed won't be sitting on its hands for long, says the market.
Traders see about an 85% chance that the Fed raises its benchmark rate by a quarter point at its next meeting on Dec. 9, according to Bloomberg data. The data comes from futures contracts that let traders bet on where the Fed sets rates. Those odds are about where they stood Tuesday, before the decision.
Further out, traders expect the Fed's rate to climb from about 3.9% now to nearly 4.7% by September 2027. That's about three more quarter-point hikes, slightly more than they expected Tuesday.
The Dec. 9 meeting is next. A hike would match what traders already expect. Another hold would mean they've gotten ahead of the Fed.
Chairman Warsh noted that while the Fed waits to assess more inflation data, some policymakers view the central bank's moves so far as beginning to take effect.
"If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said.
"If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he added. "What we decided to do was to call these questions, take stock of where we are, evaluate what we're seeing out the window, ask ourselves whether the period right in front of us is likely to provide more clarity on the appropriate protocol."

articles.title_orig: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
articles.title_zh: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Wendy’s jumped 15% at the opening bell after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the struggling burger chain
Wendy’s shares jumped 15% at the opening bell Wednesday after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores.
Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday, in a deal that would take the company private.
Wendy's, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, declined to comment Wednesday. At the end of last year, Wendy's had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries.
Wendy's, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald's and Burger King, Wendy's launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where's the beef?” ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy's fell behind. Wendy's share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.
In recent years, inflation has also hurt Wendy's and other U.S. fast-food chains, who have seen traffic from lower-income consumers fall as they raised prices to combat rising labor, food and packaging costs.
Wendy's has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations this year.
Then, last month, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
In a letter to the company’s board of directors, Peltz said going private “will deliver the best outcome for the broader stakeholder base.”
“Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture," Peltz wrote. "The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer, economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly within the QSR (quick service restaurant) burger category."
Peltz has invested in companies from Procter & Gamble and Disney to DuPont. According to a regulatory document filed Wednesday, Trian’s stake in Wendy’s totals 16.3%.
Peltz considered a take-private bid for Wendy's in 2022 but told the company in January 2023 that he had decided against it, citing its improved business momentum, according to TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles.
Charles said an independent special committee is expected to evaluate the proposal and both parties have entered into a confidentiality arrangement.
“In our view, a take-private makes sense as Wendy’s turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower-income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category,” Charles wrote Wednesday in a note to investors.
Wendy's is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results next week. Analysts expect the company to post earnings of 9 cents per share on sales of $531 million, according to FactSet.
Shares rose 88 cents to $7.01 Wednesday. They have fallen 26% since the start of this year.

articles.title_orig: War against Iran won’t distract America from China’s military buildup, Hegseth tells Pacific allies
articles.title_zh: War against Iran won’t distract America from China’s military buildup, Hegseth tells Pacific allies
articles.content_orig:
An Iranian flag is seen as missiles and air defense systems are displayed at Baharestan Square in Tehran, Iran, on September 29, 2026.
President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao , were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “ finishing the job ” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain , the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned . The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “ smuggling ” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali , an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi , strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi , chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia.
